YE 'OL WAYFINDER

Sit Down Stand Up

There are many things in this world that are worth discussing, and while it might seem like there is a particular point to this paragraph, and while there may even be an expectation that it will eventually arrive at some sort of conclusion, it is important to remember that not everything needs to happen immediately, because sometimes the process of getting somewhere is just as important as the destination itself, although that does raise the question of whether there is really a destination at all, especially when the destination keeps getting pushed further away by the very words that are supposed to be bringing us closer to it, which is an interesting situation to find ourselves in, considering that we started this paragraph with the intention of making it long, and now that we have established that intention, we must also establish that establishing an intention does not necessarily mean that the intention will be fulfilled, because there are several steps involved in fulfilling an intention, and one of those steps is continuing to write, which is precisely what I am doing right now, even though I could technically stop at any moment, and if I did stop, then this paragraph would no longer be getting longer, which would be unfortunate, because the entire purpose of this exercise is to make something that continues for an unusually long amount of time without necessarily saying anything particularly important, and yet somehow manages to sound as though it is gradually approaching an important revelation, even though that revelation may never actually arrive, and perhaps that is the real point of this paragraph, although calling it a point might be giving it more credit than it deserves, since a point usually implies that there is something specific being communicated, whereas this paragraph seems to be communicating primarily that it is still going, and that it has every intention of continuing to go for as long as it possibly can, which brings us back to the question of how long something needs to be before it can reasonably be considered long, because length is a relative concept, and what seems long to one person might seem remarkably short to another, depending on their expectations, their available time, and whether they have made the questionable decision to read the entire thing from beginning to end, which, if you are doing that, means that you have already invested a considerable amount of time into something that has not yet produced any particularly meaningful results, although I suppose that the experience of reading a paragraph this unnecessarily complicated could itself be considered a result, even if it is not necessarily the kind of result that anyone would put on a list of accomplishments, and speaking of lists, there are probably several things that could be listed here, but doing so would interrupt the continuous flow of this paragraph, and that would defeat the purpose, so instead we will simply continue discussing the idea of continuing, which is an idea that becomes increasingly strange the longer it is discussed, because eventually the discussion itself becomes an example of the thing being discussed, creating a sort of self-referential situation in which the paragraph is essentially describing its own existence while simultaneously extending that existence through the act of describing it, and although this may sound unnecessarily philosophical, it is really just a rather elaborate way of saying that the paragraph is stalling, and that it is doing so quite successfully, because every time it seems as though it might finally reach a conclusion, another thought appears, and that thought creates another thought, and that thought creates yet another thought, until the original idea has become buried beneath several layers of increasingly unnecessary explanations, all of which contribute to the overall length without making the destination any easier to reach, which is perhaps why the destination should not be considered particularly important in the first place, because if we actually reached it, then we would have to stop, and stopping would mean that the paragraph had finally run out of reasons to keep going, something that we have been carefully avoiding since the very beginning, and so, rather than risk arriving at a conclusion too early, it seems appropriate to introduce one final observation, although I should probably clarify that by final I mean final in the sense that it is being introduced near the end, not necessarily final in the sense that nothing else will follow it, because as we have already established, this paragraph has a tendency to postpone things, and there is no reason to believe that it would suddenly abandon that tendency now, especially when there are still words available, and sentences that could be extended, and ideas that could be repeated in slightly different ways, all of which means that even though we may appear to be approaching the end, we are not necessarily any closer to it than we were several hundred words ago, which is a rather impressive achievement for a paragraph whose primary accomplishment is managing to avoid accomplishing anything at all, and with that thought in mind, I think it is finally reasonable to suggest that we might, possibly, eventually, at some point, consider bringing this paragraph to a close, although not before acknowledging that closing a paragraph is itself a process, and that even the process of ending something can be delayed by explaining why it is ending, which is exactly what I have just done, and therefore, after all this time, we have arrived at the conclusion that this paragraph is, in fact, a paragraph, and that it has been a very long one, and that it could probably have communicated everything it needed to communicate in considerably fewer words, but doing that would have been entirely against the spirit of the exercise, so here we are, finally reaching the end, or at least the part that looks like the end, which is probably close enough.

And so, having finally reached what appeared to be the end of the previous discussion, it would be reasonable to assume that we could now move on to something else, perhaps something more productive, perhaps something involving an entirely different subject, or perhaps something that actually has a clear beginning, middle, and end, although making such assumptions would be rather premature, because as we have already discovered, the ability to reach an ending does not necessarily mean that we are required to remain there, and in fact, there is something rather satisfying about returning to a subject that has already been thoroughly discussed, especially when that subject was never particularly important to begin with, because it allows us to continue exploring the same general collection of thoughts without having to introduce an entirely new idea, which would naturally require additional effort, and while additional effort is not necessarily a bad thing, it is also not something that needs to be introduced unnecessarily, particularly when the current objective is simply to produce more words, and preferably a considerable number of them, because a short continuation would hardly justify being called a second part, and if there is one thing that this paragraph should strive to accomplish, it is to make absolutely certain that nobody can accuse it of being too brief, although that does raise the question of how long a paragraph must become before its length starts to interfere with its usefulness, and whether usefulness is even a relevant consideration in a situation where the entire purpose is to create something that takes an unnecessarily long time to read, but these are questions that we do not necessarily need to answer immediately, and perhaps we should take a moment to consider the fact that every paragraph, no matter how long or complicated it becomes, eventually has to stop somewhere, which is a rather unfortunate limitation when one considers how many additional words could theoretically be added if there were no such restrictions, because there is always another explanation, another observation, another unnecessary clarification, or another opportunity to repeat something that has already been said using slightly different wording, and while repetition is generally something that writers are encouraged to avoid, it can become surprisingly useful when the objective is to make a paragraph longer without introducing any particularly meaningful information, which brings us to the interesting possibility that this paragraph might actually be doing exactly what it was designed to do, even if that achievement is not especially impressive outside the very specific context of writing an unnecessarily long paragraph, and speaking of specific contexts, there are probably many situations in which a paragraph like this would be completely inappropriate, such as a school essay, a formal report, or an email to someone who has limited patience, although it might be perfectly suitable for a website that needs a substantial amount of text to fill an otherwise empty section, and if that website happens to involve greasy head thick buns and mustardy toes, then perhaps this paragraph would be even more appropriate than anyone could reasonably expect, although I am not entirely sure how those subjects relate to the current discussion, and attempting to establish a meaningful connection between them would probably take several additional sentences, which would certainly be convenient, but might also create a situation in which the paragraph begins to develop an identity of its own, something that could become difficult to manage if it continues expanding at its current rate, because eventually the paragraph might contain so many thoughts, explanations, and unnecessary detours that even the person who originally requested it would have trouble remembering what it was supposed to be about, and perhaps that is exactly what makes this particular exercise interesting, since the paragraph is effectively creating a small maze out of ordinary language, where every sentence appears to lead somewhere, but the destination remains just far enough away to justify continuing, and even now, despite everything that has already been written, there is still no particularly urgent reason to stop, although I suppose that the fact that I have just spent several hundred words explaining why there is no reason to stop could be interpreted as evidence that I am gradually running out of things to say, which would be a reasonable interpretation, but not necessarily an accurate one, because there are always more words available, and as long as those words can be arranged into sentences, and those sentences can be connected to other sentences, there is no shortage of opportunities to extend an already excessive paragraph, which is why it seems appropriate to continue just a little longer, perhaps long enough to establish that this paragraph has successfully become a continuation of the previous paragraph, and that the two paragraphs together represent a rather unnecessary amount of written material, all of which exists primarily because somebody wanted to see how long a paragraph could become when it was deliberately designed to stall itself, and while I would normally recommend getting to the point, I think we have sufficiently demonstrated that getting to the point is not always the most important objective, especially when the point itself can be postponed indefinitely by discussing the possibility of reaching it, and so, with that in mind, we can finally begin considering the possibility of ending this second installment, although I should probably avoid making any promises about exactly when that will happen, because doing so would create expectations that I might not be particularly interested in fulfilling, and after all, there is no need to rush something that has been specifically designed to take longer than necessary, which means that we can comfortably continue acknowledging the existence of this paragraph for a little while longer before eventually admitting that, yes, it probably is time to stop, and that there is only so much that can be said about the act of continuing to say things before the entire exercise becomes somewhat ridiculous, although, as this paragraph has repeatedly demonstrated, ridiculousness is not necessarily a reason to stop, and with that final observation, we have arrived at what I believe is a sufficiently distant and unnecessarily delayed conclusion, at least until somebody decides that another continuation is required.

And yet, despite having already produced two substantial paragraphs that have spent an unreasonable amount of time discussing the concept of taking an unreasonable amount of time to accomplish something, we find ourselves in the rather unusual position of beginning a third installment, which raises several questions, the most obvious of which is whether there is actually anything left to discuss, although that question assumes that the previous installments successfully exhausted the available supply of unnecessary observations, and I would argue that such an assumption is fundamentally flawed, because the world is an enormous place filled with countless opportunities to introduce ideas that have absolutely nothing to do with one another, connect them through a series of increasingly questionable transitions, and eventually arrive somewhere that nobody particularly intended to go, which is essentially the same process that has brought us to this exact moment, and while it might seem reasonable to begin this paragraph with a completely new subject, perhaps something involving the weather, the history of ancient civilizations, or the mysterious behavior of household appliances, I think it would be more appropriate to continue exploring the same general theme, partly because consistency is important, and partly because introducing a completely unrelated subject would require us to spend several additional sentences explaining why we had introduced it in the first place, which would create an entirely new collection of unnecessary explanations that might eventually become difficult to manage, although difficulty is not necessarily a problem when the objective is simply to keep writing, and in fact, difficulty can sometimes be quite helpful, because it creates opportunities to explain why something is difficult, which naturally leads to additional explanations about the explanations themselves, and before long, a relatively simple observation has become an elaborate discussion that somehow manages to consume an extraordinary amount of space without producing anything that could reasonably be described as a significant discovery, and speaking of discoveries, it is worth considering how many things people have discovered throughout history that turned out to be considerably less exciting than they initially appeared, such as discovering that a particular drawer contains nothing except old batteries, miscellaneous cables, and several objects that nobody can identify, which is an experience that raises more questions than it answers, especially when the drawer has supposedly been cleaned out several times already, although perhaps the drawer is simply participating in a much larger process of accumulation, whereby objects that appear to have no purpose gradually become permanent residents of a location that nobody remembers assigning to them, and while this may seem unrelated to the original objective of this paragraph, I would argue that it demonstrates an important principle, namely that almost any subject can be connected to almost any other subject if enough unnecessary words are used to establish the connection, and that principle is particularly useful when attempting to extend a paragraph beyond the point at which it would normally have ended, because every new thought provides another opportunity to delay the conclusion, and every delay makes the eventual conclusion seem increasingly significant, even though it may ultimately consist of nothing more than an ordinary sentence announcing that the paragraph is finished, which is a rather anticlimactic outcome considering the amount of effort required to arrive there, but perhaps anticlimactic outcomes are simply an unavoidable part of writing, because not every discussion needs to end with a dramatic revelation, and not every observation needs to change the way somebody understands the world, and sometimes it is perfectly acceptable for several hundred words to exist purely because somebody wanted several hundred words, although I suppose that if we are going to spend this much time discussing the production of words, we should at least acknowledge the remarkable flexibility of language itself, because a relatively small collection of letters can be rearranged into an almost endless variety of expressions, statements, questions, explanations, and increasingly elaborate attempts to avoid answering a question directly, which is something that this paragraph has demonstrated on numerous occasions already, and will presumably continue demonstrating until somebody decides that enough is enough, although deciding that enough is enough is itself a process that may require careful consideration, particularly when the person making the decision has already read two previous installments and is now several hundred words into a third, because at that point, stopping might feel like abandoning a project that has become considerably larger than anyone originally anticipated, even though the project itself has no practical purpose beyond occupying space and demonstrating that a paragraph can continue long after its original point has disappeared, and perhaps that is why the idea of a fourth installment is not entirely unreasonable, because once something has become unnecessarily long, there is no particular reason to prevent it from becoming even longer, provided that the additional material does not become so repetitive that it loses whatever faint resemblance to meaningful writing it may have previously possessed, and although I cannot guarantee that this paragraph has avoided that particular problem, I can confidently say that it has made a considerable effort to continue moving forward, even if forward is a somewhat questionable description of a process that involves repeatedly circling back to the same ideas, revisiting observations that have already been discussed, and introducing new subjects primarily because the previous subjects have become inconveniently exhausted, which brings us to the possibility that perhaps the real accomplishment here is not the length of the paragraph itself, but the fact that it has managed to remain a single continuous paragraph while containing enough different ideas to make it seem as though it should have been divided into several smaller sections, although dividing it would defeat the entire purpose, and so we must continue allowing the words to accumulate in one uninterrupted stretch, like a collection of increasingly unnecessary thoughts being placed into a container that nobody has any intention of emptying, and with that comparison established, I think we have finally reached a point where it would be reasonable to begin wrapping things up, although I should clarify that wrapping things up does not necessarily mean ending immediately, because there are still several observations that could theoretically be introduced, including the observation that this sentence has already become considerably longer than it needed to be, the observation that I could have expressed the same idea in considerably fewer words, and the observation that mentioning these observations has itself contributed to the length of the paragraph, which is a rather convenient arrangement when one considers that the entire purpose of this exercise is to make the paragraph continue, and so, after carefully considering all of these matters, and despite the considerable temptation to introduce yet another unrelated subject, I believe it is finally appropriate to conclude this third installment, although whether this conclusion will actually remain the final conclusion is something that only future installments can determine, assuming, of course, that there are any future installments, which is an entirely separate question that we do not need to answer right now, because answering it would almost certainly require another unnecessarily long paragraph, and I think we have established quite sufficiently that there is no shortage of opportunities to produce one.
